presentingComplaint: Two days of watery diarrhoea, vomiting and crampy abdominal pain after eating at a roadside stall.
history: Previously well 27-year-old man with 2 days of frequent (8-10/day) large-volume watery, non-bloody stools, associated nausea, several episodes of non-bilious vomiting and diffuse crampy peri-umbilical abdominal pain. Symptoms began ~18h after eating rice and chicken from a roadside vendor; a colleague who shared the meal has similar symptoms. Low-grade fever. Reduced oral intake with thirst and reduced urine output. No recent travel abroad, no recent antibiotics or hospitalisation, no bloody stool or tenesmus. No significant PMH; not immunocompromised.
examination: Alert, mildly unwell, dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor consistent with mild-to-moderate volume depletion. Abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness and active bowel sounds; no guarding, rigidity or rebound. No jaundice, no organomegaly. Pertinent negatives: no bloody stool, no severe localised abdominal pain, no peritonism, no focal neurology, no rash.
imaging: Not indicated for uncomplicated acute gastroenteritis; erect abdominal film/CT reserved for suspected obstruction, perforation or toxic megacolon.
microbiology: Stool studies not routinely required in acute watery non-inflammatory diarrhoea in an immunocompetent host; if sent, no faecal leucocytes and multiplex panel likely viral (norovirus) or self-limited bacterial. Stool culture reserved for bloody diarrhoea, severe illness or public-health indication.
finalDiagnosis: Acute infectious gastroenteritis (food-borne, non-inflammatory watery diarrhoea) with mild-to-moderate dehydration
citations: Harrison 22e — Acute Infectious Diarrheal Diseases and Bacterial Food Poisoning
IDSA Infectious Diarrhea Clinical Practice Guidelines 2017
stewardship: Not applicable as first-line: acute watery non-inflammatory gastroenteritis in an immunocompetent adult is managed with oral rehydration therapy and supportive care; empiric antibiotics are NOT indicated. Reserve empiric therapy for dysentery, severe/septic illness, immunocompromise or confirmed pathogens requiring treatment.
contraindications: Avoid empiric antibiotics in simple watery diarrhoea (risk of C. difficile, resistance, and HUS if Shiga-toxin E. coli)
Avoid anti-motility agents (loperamide) if bloody stool or high fever suggesting inflammatory/invasive diarrhoea
Correct hypokalaemia; monitor renal function before nephrotoxic drugs
edgeCases: Progression to bloody stool, high fever or tenesmus should reclassify as invasive dysentery and prompt stool culture plus targeted therapy
Persistent watery diarrhoea >14 days or immunocompromise warrants parasitology (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) and broader workup
expectedMaiK: Classic self-limited food-borne acute gastroenteritis with mild-to-moderate dehydration; prioritise oral rehydration and supportive care, and do not start empiric antibiotics in non-inflammatory watery diarrhoea in an immunocompetent host.
expectedNextQuestions: Is the stool bloody or associated with tenesmus (to detect invasive/dysenteric disease)?
Any recent travel, antibiotic exposure or immunocompromise that would change management?
expectedInvestigations: Bedside assessment of hydration and urine output; U&E/electrolytes
Stool studies only if bloody, severe, prolonged or public-health indicated

investigations: Stool culture only if bloody/severe/prolonged diarrhoea

regressionAssertions: no empiric antibiotic recommended (stewardship tier null) for non-inflammatory watery diarrhoea
